title: Retrieval Practice "in the Wild": Teachers' Reported Use of Retrieval Practice in the Classroom https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/mbe.12420
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 17, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers Bates and Shea's survey of 153 English teachers on how they actually use retrieval practice, moving beyond lab findings to look at real classroom implementation. Almost all surveyed teachers reported regularly using retrieval practice, often via quizzes and short-answer questions, even where it isn't mandated by school policy. Beyond revision, many teachers use it as an active learning strategy to connect prior material to the current lesson, and some reported behavioural side-benefits — settling a class at the start of a lesson. Barton highlights that verbal questioning, despite being ubiquitous in classrooms, remains under-researched as a form of retrieval practice, and that teachers frequently reteach content after retrieval activities without clear evidence on how effective that reteaching is. The piece closes by calling for more classroom-based, rather than self-reported, research into how retrieval practice is actually placed and used within lessons.
points: Retrieval practice has become a genuinely widespread, teacher-driven classroom habit, independent of formal school policy mandates.
Verbal questioning — one of the most common classroom practices — is largely unstudied as a form of retrieval practice, leaving a real research gap.
Some teachers report retrieval practice helps settle a class and set the tone at the start of a lesson, a possible behavioural side-benefit worth further study.
Reteaching content after weak retrieval performance is common practice, but its effectiveness beyond retrieval-plus-feedback is not yet well evidenced.
